title: Gregorian to Lunar Converter: Leap Months and Year Boundaries
description: Lunar converter: no Gregorian year limit, lunar side 1900–2100, leap-month box errors when a year has none, days fixed 1–30, solar terms only on the day.
content:
On this site the Gregorian–lunar converter converts dates locally in the browser with lunar-javascript: the Gregorian side splits the date into y, m and d and hands them to Solar.fromYmd(), while the lunar side writes a leap month as a negative month number and hands it to Lunar.fromYmd(). Both panels compute the right answer, but the year range, the leap months and the legality of the thirtieth day are not symmetric.

1. Converted on load: each panel computes its own result

The page-level const now = new Date() is evaluated exactly once; then setTodaySolar() fills the Gregorian input with today and calls convertToLunar(), while setTodayLunar() uses Solar.fromDate(now).getLunar() to back-fill the three dropdowns and calls convertToSolar(). When the page opens, both panels already show a result — you never have to press a button.

Pin the browser's fake clock to 2026-11-10T03:00:00Z and set the browser time zone to UTC, and the Gregorian panel shows three rows: “Lunar: tenth lunar month, day two, year 2026”, “Sexagenary: year of Bing-wu · month of Ji-hai · day of Wu-zi” and “Zodiac: Horse”; the lunar panel is back-filled to 2026, month 10, day 2, and its result is “Gregorian: 2026-11-10 (Tuesday)”. Both status lines read “Conversion complete”, with the class status-msg show success.

There is one space in the copy that is easy to copy wrongly: the template for the lunar row is ${getYearInChinese()}年 ${getMonthInChinese()}月${getDayInChinese()}, with a space after the year unit and none after the month unit, so it renders with a gap between the year and the rest, not as one unbroken string. On a day that is not a solar term the result has only 3 rows; only a solar-term day gains a fourth.

2. An asymmetric range: the Gregorian side has no year limit

The Gregorian field is a native input[type=date] with no min or max in the code; the three dropdowns on the lunar side are filled by script: the year loop for (let y = 1900; y <= 2100; y++) gives 201 entries, the month list gives 12, and the days come from the hard-coded CHINESE_DAYS with 30 entries. The two directions therefore do not cover the same interval.

Try it on the page and the gap is immediate: type 1899-12-31 into the Gregorian field and it still converts to “Lunar: winter month, day twenty-nine, year 1899”, with sexagenary “year of Ji-hai · month of Bing-zi · day of Gui-you” and zodiac “Pig”; type 2101-01-01 and it converts to “Lunar: twelfth month, day two, year 2100”, with zodiac “Monkey”. In other words the Gregorian input can cross 1900–2100 freely and the library still returns a result.

The reverse direction is constrained: the lunar dropdown can go back only as far as the first day of the first month of 1900, which converts to 1900-01-31 (Wednesday); the latest year you can pick is 2100, and the twelfth month of 2100 has only 29 days, so picking “thirty” raises an error, while the twenty-ninth day of that month converts to 2101-01-28 (Friday) — a result year already beyond the dropdown's ceiling of 2100.

The Hong Kong Observatory's Gregorian–lunar conversion table covers 1901 to 2100 and notes that, because moon phases and solar-term times calculated decades ahead may be a few minutes out, a date in the table may be off by one day when a new moon or a solar-term moment falls close to midnight. The tool's range is 1900–2100, one year earlier than the observatory's 1901 at the lower end; neither of them can be treated as “any year can be looked up”.

3. Leap months: one checkbox plus a negative month

The lunar side has no separate “which month is repeated” selector — only a “Leap month” checkbox, and the conversion writes Lunar.fromYmd(y, leap ? -m : m, d). A negative month is this library's convention for leap months: getMonth() returning -6 means a leap sixth month, and getMonthInChinese() returns a two-character string whose first character is already the word “leap”; the eleventh and twelfth months of an ordinary year return the single characters for “winter” and “twelfth” instead.

Before ticking it you have to know whether that year has a leap month at all. 2026 has none (LunarYear.fromYear(2026).getLeapMonth() returns 0), so ticking the leap box and picking month 6, day 15 makes the library throw Error: wrong lunar year 2026 month -6, and the page catches it and shows “That lunar date does not exist; check whether the leap-month box is ticked”. It only works in a year that really has one: 2025 has a leap sixth month, so with the box ticked the first day of month 6 converts to 2025-07-25 (Friday), while without it the same fields give 2025-06-25 (Wednesday) — 30 days apart, exactly the length of the non-leap sixth month.

Between 1900 and 2100 there are 74 years that contain a leap month; in recent decades they are 2020 (leap fourth month), 2023 (leap second month), 2025 (leap sixth month), 2028 (leap fifth month), 2031 (leap third month) and 2033 (leap eleventh month). A leap month can also be only 29 days long: the first day of the leap eleventh month of 2033 is 2033-12-22, and the thirtieth day of it throws only 29 days in lunar year 2033 month -11.

The origin of leap months is on the observatory's 24 solar terms page: the lunisolar calendar requires every month to contain a principal solar term (zhongqi), and a month that lacks one becomes a leap repeat of the month before it; 19 tropical years hold 228 principal terms and 235 synodic months, so exactly 7 months have none, and those become the leap months.

4. Days fixed at thirty: picking “thirty” in a short month fails

The day dropdown is 30 hard-coded options and is not rebuilt when the month changes: switch the lunar month to 2 and the day list still has 30 entries, with “thirty” still selectable. In 2026 the short months are 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 12 (29 days each) and the long months are 1, 3, 6, 9, 10 and 11 (30 days each).

Pick “thirty” in a short month and the library throws only 29 days in lunar year 2026 month 2, yet the page shows the same sentence as before: “That lunar date does not exist; check whether the leap-month box is ticked”. The message mentions leap months only, never short months, so it is easy to misread as “there is no leap month this year”. Long months behave normally: the thirtieth day of the ninth month of 2026 → 2026-11-08 (Sunday).

Both kinds of failure only change the status line; they do not clear the result box. Convert 2026-08-02 (Sunday) successfully first, then set the lunar side to 2026, month 4, day 30 (month 4 has only 29 days) and press “To Gregorian”: the status line turns red while the result box still reads “Gregorian: 2026-08-02 (Sunday)”. Clearing the Gregorian input works the same way: the prompt “Please choose a Gregorian date” appears and the previous lunar result stays exactly where it was.

5. Solar terms appear only on the day itself

getJieQi() returns a solar-term name only on the day of that term; the day before and the day after both return an empty string. Of the 30 days of November 2026 only two hit: 7 November (2026-11-07), “Lidong (Start of Winter)”, and 22 November (2026-11-22), “Xiaoxue (Minor Snow)”. On 7 November the result has 4 rows, with an extra “Solar term: Lidong (Start of Winter)”; on 6 November there are only 3 rows and the lunar date is the twenty-eighth day of the ninth month of 2026.

So the solar-term row does not mean “Lidong has already passed” — it means “today is exactly Lidong”, and the row disappears once the day is over. Crossing the year boundary works the same way: 2026-12-22 returns “Dongzhi (Winter Solstice)” and 2027-01-05 returns “Xiaohan (Minor Cold)”. Internally the library generates 31 solar-term entries in one go, covering the neighbouring years, so boundary dates still get a name.

The observatory's solar-term page gives the conversion rule: the 24 solar terms split the 360-degree ecliptic into equal parts 15 degrees of longitude apart, with the spring equinox at 0 degrees, Qingming at 15 degrees and Lidong at 225 degrees. That explains why the same term falls on a different Gregorian day in different years: it follows the position of the sun, not a fixed month and day.

6. The year boundary is the first day of the first lunar month; the month pillar changes at solar terms

The page's getYearInGanZhi() and getYearShengXiao() both switch at the first day of the first lunar month, not at Lichun (Start of Spring). In 2026 Lichun falls on 4 February, and on that day the result still shows the sexagenary year “Yi-si” and the zodiac “Snake”; only on 17 February, the lunar New Year's Day, does it become “Bing-wu” and “Horse”. The same library also has getYearInGanZhiByLiChun() and getYearShengXiaoByLiChun(), which are already “Bing-wu” and “Horse” on 4 February — the page does not use that pair.

The month pillar, by contrast, does change at solar terms: 2026-02-03 is the month of Ji-chou, Lichun on 4 February turns it into Geng-yin, and Jingzhe (Awakening of Insects) on 5 March turns it into Xin-mao. Within a single day the “year” follows the lunar year while the “month” follows the solar terms, and the two boundaries coexist, which makes the sexagenary combinations around the New Year the easiest to misread.

So the answer to “what zodiac is 2026” depends on the convention: by the lunar year the page displays, 4 February to 16 February 2026 still belongs to the Snake and the Horse starts on 17 February; by the Lichun convention the switch to the Horse happens on 4 February.

7. The “Today” button only knows the moment of page load, and the time zone picks the day

Because now is evaluated at module top level, the “Today” button reads the instant the page loaded, not the instant you click. Freeze the clock at 2026-11-10T03:00:00Z, advance 24 hours after load (the page's Date is now 2026-11-11) and click “Today”: the input still holds 2026-11-10 and the result is still day two of the tenth month. Only reloading the page makes it 2026-11-11 and day three of the tenth lunar month.

The browser time zone also decides that default date. At the same instant, 2026-11-10T20:00:00Z, a UTC context reads 10 November and fills in 2026-11-10; switch to Asia/Shanghai (UTC+8, where it is already 04:00 on 11 November) and the default becomes 2026-11-11, day three of the tenth lunar month. The conversion buttons in both panels work in either run; the only difference is that “today” is taken from local time — MDN's Date reference lists getFullYear(), getMonth() and getDate() as methods that return values in local time, and those are exactly the three the page uses to read the year, month and day.

The conversion itself is not affected by the time zone: both panels pass an explicit year, month and day to the library, with no Date parsing in between. So when you discuss a lunar date across time zones, confirm which zone's “today” the other person means.

8. Boundaries and limits

This tool is a “given year, month and day → given year, month and day” converter: it saves nothing, keeps no history, and does not explain the folk meaning behind a date. A few hard boundaries:

  • The lunar side's year list is fixed to 1900–2100 (201 entries), so beyond that range you can only come in from the Gregorian side; the Gregorian side has no min or max, so 1899 and 2101 both convert — the lunar year that 1899-12-31 converts to cannot be selected in the dropdown (which starts at 1900), while the date that 2101-01-01 converts to can still be selected back as 2100, month 12 on the lunar side.
  • Leap months are expressed by a checkbox, and you must already know which month is repeated in that year; ticking it in a year with no leap month produces an error that only says the date does not exist, never that the year has no leap month.
  • Days are fixed to 1–30, and the error for picking “thirty” in a short month reuses the same sentence as the leap-month error, which never mentions month length, so you have to check the month's real length yourself.
  • The solar-term row appears only on the day itself; it does not show the next term or how many days remain until it.
  • The sexagenary year and the zodiac switch at the first day of the first lunar month, which differs from the Lichun convention; the page offers no way to switch.
  • “Today” takes the local time at the instant the page loaded, so after midnight it still fills in the old date and only a refresh updates it.
  • When a conversion fails the result box keeps the previous successful result and only the status line changes colour, so read the status line when you read a result.

When you need a different convention you can chain tools: for the gap between two Gregorian dates use date difference, to look up a zodiac sign by date use zodiac lookup, and for the Gregorian month layout and public-holiday arrangement use the calendar. This article only describes how this page behaved across this run's 26 browser cases and 15 Node checks; it does not touch date selection, auspiciousness or any other folk judgement.

faqs.q: How do I convert between Gregorian and lunar dates?
faqs.a: To go from Gregorian to lunar, hand the year, month and day to Solar.fromYmd(y, m, d).getLunar(); to go from lunar to Gregorian, hand them to Lunar.fromYmd(y, m, d).getSolar(), with a leap month written as a negative month number, so -6 means a leap sixth month. The tool on this site does both steps locally in the browser, without any network call.

faqs.q: Why does ticking “Leap month” in 2026 say the date does not exist?
faqs.a: 2026 has no leap month. The library's LunarYear.fromYear(2026).getLeapMonth() returns 0, and passing a negative month then throws Error: wrong lunar year 2026 month -6, which the page always renders as “That lunar date does not exist; check whether the leap-month box is ticked”. To convert a leap month you first have to pick a year that has one, such as 2025 with its leap sixth month or 2028 with its leap fifth month.

faqs.q: Why does the lunar day dropdown always have 30 entries, and why does picking “thirty” fail?
faqs.a: The day dropdown is built from the hard-coded CHINESE_DAYS list and is fixed to 1–30; switching the month does not rebuild it. Lunar months have either 29 or 30 days, and picking “thirty” in a 29-day month makes the library throw only 29 days in lunar year 2026 month 2, after which the page shows the same sentence about the lunar date not existing. The 29-day months in 2026 are 2, 4, 5, 7, 8 and 12.

faqs.q: Why can the Gregorian field take 1899 while the lunar year cannot be selected?
faqs.a: The Gregorian input is a native input[type=date] with no min or max in the code, so 1899-12-31 still converts to the twenty-ninth day of the winter month of 1899; the lunar year dropdown is generated by script from 1900 to 2100 as 201 entries, so out-of-range years simply have no option and can only be reached from the Gregorian side.

faqs.q: When does the solar-term row appear?
faqs.a: Only on the day of that solar term. Among the 30 days of November 2026 only 2026-11-07 (Lidong, Start of Winter) and 2026-11-22 (Xiaoxue, Minor Snow) make getJieQi() return a name; every other day returns an empty string, so the result has just the three rows for lunar date, sexagenary cycle and zodiac.

faqs.q: Why does the “Today” button not give today?
faqs.a: The page evaluates const now = new Date() once, at load, and the “Today” button uses that frozen value. Clicking it after midnight still fills in the date from the day the page loaded, and only a refresh updates it; the value is also local time, so the same instant can be a different day under UTC and Asia/Shanghai.

focus: Both panels of the Gregorian–lunar converter use lunar-javascript to convert locally: the Gregorian side has no year limit while the lunar side offers only the 201 years from 1900 to 2100; leap months are expressed by one checkbox plus a negative month, and ticking it in a year without a leap month throws an error and always shows the same “that lunar date does not exist” message; days are fixed to 1–30, so picking “thirty” in a 29-day month fails in the same way; getJieQi() returns a name only on the day of the term; the sexagenary year and zodiac switch at the first day of the first lunar month while the month pillar switches at solar terms; and the “Today” button reads the local time of the moment the page loaded.
